titleText.es: Es difícil caber en el asiento de atrás con mi androide RealDoll cuando ambos llevamos puestos los jetpacks.
titleText.en: It's hard to fit in the backseat of my flying car with my android Realdoll when we're both wearing jetpacks.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish title text is preserved exactly from the archive, including the branded names RealDoll and jetpacks. The English field preserves the official title text. The Spanish raster localizes the official 3D shooter more generally as VIDEOJUEGO 3D and names ANGRY BIRDS in the final warning; those technical and game-title labels, plus the year 2011, are audited exclusions. OCR's PAR, UGAR, 31, INTERRUMPI, and Tio are corrected to the visible PARA, JUGAR, 3D, INTERRUMPÍ, and TÍO.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Volador describes something that flies or is designed to fly. It changes to voladora with a feminine singular noun and adds -es in the plural.

example.en: They designed a flying vehicle.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Quejando is the -ando form used inside quejarse, “to complain.” Its matching marker appears separately before a conjugated helper: te estás quejando.

example.es: Siempre se está quejando del ruido.
example.en: He is always complaining about the noise.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Compras is the plural of compra. In hacer compras, it refers to shopping or making purchases.

example.es: Hicimos las compras por la mañana.
example.en: We did the shopping in the morning.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Lees is the present form of leer for one familiar listener.

example.en: You read many books.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: you were (helper for an action in progress)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Estabas is the informal-singular imperfect form of estar. Before an -ando or -iendo form, it presents what the listener was doing in the background.

example.en: You were reading when I called.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Jugar means taking part in a game. It is commonly followed by a before the game or activity.

example.en: We are going to play chess.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: no separate English word; required after jugar before a game
cardDefinitions.noteEn: When jugar names the game being played, Spanish normally uses a before it. Before el, a and el combine as al.

example.es: Los niños juegan a un juego nuevo.
example.en: The children play a new game.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Videojuego combines vídeo and juego into the standard word for an electronic game.

example.en: They bought a cooperative video game.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Interrumpí is the completed-past form of interrumpir for the speaker. The written accent marks the stressed final syllable.

example.en: I interrupted the meeting by mistake.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Hubiera is a special past form of haber. In a counterfactual result, it can combine with a completed-action form as an accepted alternative to habría: hubiera sido can mean “would have been.”

example.en: It would have been better to wait.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Videollamada combines vídeo and llamada for a call in which participants can see one another.

example.es: Tenemos una videollamada a las tres.
example.en: We have a video call at three.

cardDefinitions.answerEn: were wearing; had on (in an unreal condition)
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Llevara is a special -ra form of llevar used for an imagined condition. With puesto or puesta, it describes clothing that someone has on.

example.es: Si llevara abrigo, no tendría frío.
example.en: If I were wearing a coat, I would not be cold.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Puesta follows a form of llevar to describe clothing being worn. It matches the clothing noun: puesto for masculine singular and puesta for feminine singular.

example.en: She is wearing a blue jacket.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Camiseta usually names a T-shirt or light casual shirt.

example.en: He is wearing a white T-shirt.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Estrellarías is the conditional form used with te for the pronominal verb estrellarse, “to crash.” The ending -ías marks one familiar listener.

example.en: Without brakes, you would crash.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Tecleando is the -ando form of teclear, pressing keys to enter text. Context can make it typing at a keyboard or texting on a phone.

example.en: She crossed the street while texting.

cardDefinitions.noteEn: Jugando is the -ando form of jugar. It can name a simultaneous action and is followed by a before the game being played.

example.es: Pasó la tarde jugando al dominó.
example.en: He spent the afternoon playing dominoes.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone shops or makes purchases?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a matching form of hacer followed by compras.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Hacer changes for the person and time: hago compras, haces compras, hicimos compras. Compras remains plural and names the shopping activity or purchases.

example.en: We do our shopping on Saturdays.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you name the game that someone plays?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a form of jugar, then a, then the game.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Jugar changes for the player and time. A links it to the game. If the game has masculine article el, a + el must contract to al: jugar al tenis. With an indefinite article, keep a un or a una.

example.es: Marta juega a un juego de cartas y Luis juega al tenis.
example.en: Marta plays a card game and Luis plays tennis.

cardDefinitions.questionEn: How do you say that someone has an item of clothing on?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use a matching form of llevar followed by puesto, puesta, puestos, or puestas and the clothing item.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: Llevar changes for the wearer and time. Puesto changes to match the clothing noun in gender and number: lleva puesto un abrigo, lleva puestas unas botas.

example.en: Ana is wearing a hat.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: hubiera + participio ... si + forma hipotética en -ra
cardDefinitions.questionEn: How can you say that an unreal situation now would have produced a different earlier result, using hubiera?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: Use hubiera plus a completed-action form for the imagined result, and use si plus a special -ra form for the unreal current condition.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The condition's -ra form is called the imperfect subjunctive: tener becomes tuviera. The result uses the past subjunctive helper hubiera plus a participle, a completed-action form such as ido or visto. In result clauses, this hubiera form is an accepted alternative to habría: hubiera ido and habría ido can both mean “would have gone.”

example.es: Hubiera ido contigo si tuviera tiempo.
example.en: I would have gone with you if I had time.

cardDefinitions.promptEs: coche volador · teléfono · videojuego · videollamada · estrellarse
cardDefinitions.questionEn: Why does the reply argue that a flying car would be unsafe despite impressive modern technology?
cardDefinitions.answerEn: The phone already combines shopping, books, 3D games, and video calls, but the user's distraction by that same device would make a flying car dangerous.
cardDefinitions.noteEn: The complaint treats flying cars as the missing sign of the future while ignoring capabilities that already arrived in a handheld device. The final warning turns that wonder into a safety problem: typing or gaming while piloting would add airborne consequences to familiar distracted-driving behavior.

example.es: La tecnología nueva no elimina el riesgo de usarla sin atención.
example.en: New technology does not remove the risk of using it inattentively.

applications.explanationEn: Que continues the description of the earlier phone, while estabas usando supplies the complete action that describes it.
Estabas matches one familiar listener in past background time, and usando supplies the ongoing action.
Estabas uses the imperfect to frame the listener's use as background already in progress.
Para introduces the purpose, and jugar remains in its dictionary form.
Jugar names the activity, a provides its required link, and un videojuego fills the game slot.
Hasta que introduces a completed factual endpoint, and interrumpí uses an ordinary completed-past statement form.
Interrumpí uses the preterite to present the interruption as the completed event that advances the story.
Lo and que refer neutrally to the unnamed thing or situation described next.
